title: Chevalley scheme-theoretic line stabilizer theorem
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $G$ an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and $H\subseteq G$ a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. There exist a nonzero finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $E$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], a rational representation $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(E)$, and a one-dimensional $k$-subspace $D\subseteq E$ such that, for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, $$H(A)=\{g\in G(A):\rho_A(g)(D\otimes_k A)=D\otimes_k A\}.$$ Here a rational representation is a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes; after a basis choice $\mathrm{GL}(E)=\mathrm{GL}_{\dim E,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group], and its $A$-points act as the $A$-linear automorphisms of $E\otimes_k A$. The equality is natural in $A$; no smoothness or reducedness of $G$ or $H$ is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 (Chevalley), printed pp.94--95, and Remark 4.30, printed p.96 (scheme-theoretic stabilizer on every k-algebra).

proof.text: Put $C=k[G]$. By [def-weil-closed-immersion], $H=\operatorname{Spec}(C/I)$ for an ideal $I$. By [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra], $C$ is a finite-type $k$-algebra. A field is Noetherian since its only ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$; hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] and [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] give finitely many ideal generators $f_1,\ldots,f_s$ of $I$ (the empty list is permitted).

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text: The coproduct and counit on $C$ have the coalgebra identities by [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. Apply [lem-sfb-coalgebra-finite-subcoalgebra] to $\{1,f_1,\ldots,f_s\}$ to obtain a finite-dimensional subspace $V\subset C$ containing these elements and satisfying $\Delta(V)\subset V\otimes_k V\subset V\otimes_k C$. In particular $V\ne0$. The restricted coproduct is a coaction, so [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] gives a rational representation $r:G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$, with $r_A(x)(v\otimes1)=(1\otimes x)\Delta(v)$ for $x:C\to A$. This is the restricted right regular representation used in Milne's proof; the existing subcoalgebra lemma supplies a stronger form of his Proposition 4.7.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text: Put $W=I\cap V$, choose a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $W$, and extend it to $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $V$. Write $\Delta(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes a_{ij}$ and let $q:C\to C/I$. The subgroup laws [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] imply $(q\otimes q)\Delta(e_j)=0$ and $\epsilon(e_j)=0$ for $j\le d$: multiplication of two $H$-points and the identity factor through $H$. Here the coordinate maps are the pullbacks in [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. Since $q(e_{d+1}),\ldots,q(e_n)$ are linearly independent, applying their coordinate functionals (extended to a basis of $C/I$) to the first tensor factor gives $q(a_{ij})=0$ for $i>d$, $j\le d$. Thus all these $a_{ij}$ lie in $I$. Conversely, the counit identity gives $e_j=\sum_i\epsilon(e_i)a_{ij}=\sum_{i>d}\epsilon(e_i)a_{ij}$ for $j\le d$. Since the $f_t$ lie in $W$, the $e_j$, $j\le d$, generate $I$ as an ideal. Therefore $I=(a_{ij}:i>d,\ j\le d)$.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text: Fix any commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$, represented by $x:C\to A$. By [def-weil-closed-immersion], $g\in H(A)$ if and only if $x(I)=0$, equivalently $x(a_{ij})=0$ for $i>d$, $j\le d$. By the action formula of [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary], these are precisely the coefficients of $r_A(g)e_j$ outside $W_A$. Consequently $r_A(g)W_A=W_A$ implies $g\in H(A)$. Conversely, if $g\in H(A)$, both $g$ and $g^{-1}$ belong to $H(A)$ by [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], so both $r_A(g)$ and its inverse carry $W_A$ into itself, proving equality. We have proved $H(A)=\{g:r_A(g)W_A=W_A\}$ without replacing $A$ by a field or taking radicals.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text: Set $E=\bigwedge_k^d V$ and $w=e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_d$ (for $d=0$, $w=1$), using [def-weil-pbc-exterior-algebra]. The free exterior basis [lem-weil-pbc-exterior-power-free-basis] shows that $E$ is finite-dimensional, $w\ne0$, and $D=kw\subset E$ is a line. It also identifies $E\otimes_k A$ with $\bigwedge_A^d(V\otimes_k A)$: the map sends each base-changed ordered wedge basis vector to the same ordered wedge, hence sends a basis bijectively to a basis. For each $g\in G(A)$, the tensor-algebra map induced by $r_A(g)$ preserves the ideal generated by $v\otimes v$, so induces $\rho_A(g)=\bigwedge^d r_A(g)$. It respects multiplication and inverses because this holds on pure wedges. Its matrix entries are minors of those of $r_A(g)$, so the maps are natural in $A$. By [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary], this finite-dimensional natural representation is a homomorphism of group schemes $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(E)$.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text:
We check the exterior-line test directly in these bases, as in Milne Lemma 4.28. For any $A$, [lem-weil-pbc-exterior-power-free-basis] gives
$$W_A=\{v\in V_A:w\wedge v=0\},$$
since for $v=\sum b_i e_i$, $w\wedge v=\sum_{i>d}b_i(e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_d\wedge e_i)$, with distinct basis vectors. If $\alpha=r_A(g)$ preserves $W_A$ with equality, its restriction is an automorphism of $W_A$; taking its top exterior power gives $(\bigwedge^d\alpha)D_A=D_A$. Conversely, this line equality means $(\bigwedge^d\alpha)w=cw$ for a unit $c\in A$: the restriction to the free rank-one module $D_A$ is bijective. For $v\in W_A$,
$$0=(\bigwedge^{d+1}\alpha)(w\wedge v)=cw\wedge\alpha(v),$$
so $\alpha(v)\in W_A$. Apply the identical calculation to $\alpha^{-1}$ to obtain equality. Thus $\rho_A(g)D_A=D_A$ if and only if $r_A(g)W_A=W_A$. These computations use the quotient construction in [def-weil-pbc-exterior-algebra] and work also for $d=0$, when $w\wedge v=v$, and for $d=n$, when $W_A=V_A$.

source.place: Theorem 4.27 and Lemma 4.28, printed pp.94–95; Remark 4.30, printed p.96.

proof.text: Combining steps 4 and 6 gives the required equality for every $A$, with the single pair $(E,D)$ constructed over $k$. All matrices and their exterior minors are evaluated by the map $C\to A$; applying a $k$-algebra map $A\to B$ applies it entrywise, and [def-weil-module-base-change] sends the chosen basis of $D_A$ to that of $D_B$. Thus these equalities describe the same subfunctor of $G$ and are natural in $A$, as asserted in Milne Remark 4.30. The nonzero vector $w\in E$ ensures $E\ne0$. No step imposed smoothness, reducedness, or a characteristic restriction.
